definition: Roth v. United States, 354 U.S. 476 (1957), was a U.S. Supreme Court decision holding that obscenity is not protected speech under the First Amendment. Samuel Roth, a New York bookseller, was convicted under a federal statute prohibiting the mailing of “obscene, lewd, lascivious, or filthy” publications. Roth argued that the statute violated the constitutional guarantee of freedom of speech and press. Writing for the majority, Justice William J. Brennan, Jr. held that obscene material is “utterly without redeeming social importance” and therefore falls outside the scope of First Amendment protection. The Court reasoned that the Amendment was intended to protect ideas of social value, not speech appealing solely to prurient interest. Justice William O. Douglas dissented, warning that the decision vested the government with excessive discretion to judge morality and suppress controversial or unpopular expression. The Roth standard was later superseded by Miller v. California, 413 U.S. 15 (1973), which established a three-part test for determining obscenity: rogatory letters / Roth v.
